title: Module Overview: Galois Group of cos(π/7)
content: The file establishes |Gal(8X³−4X²−4X+1/ℚ)| = 3, mirroring the companion proof for cos(20°) = cos(π/9) in AngleTrisectionCos20Gal.lean. The key algebraic relationships between the three roots come from trigonometric identities: cos(5π/7) = −cos(2π/7) = 1−2cos²(π/7) (double-angle), and cos(3π/7) = 4cos³(π/7)−3cos(π/7) ≡ 2cos²(π/7)−cos(π/7)−1/2 modulo the minimal polynomial (triple-angle). The proof strategy: show all three roots lie in ℚ(α), hence splitting field = ℚ(α) with [ℚ(α):ℚ] = 3, giving |Gal| = 3. The only difference from the cos(20°) proof is the Eisenstein prime: 7 here vs 3 for cos(π/9).
mathContext: Polynomial: $p(X) = 8X^3 - 4X^2 - 4X + 1$ with roots $\alpha = \cos(\pi/7)$, $\beta = \cos(3\pi/7)$, $\gamma = \cos(5\pi/7)$. The Eisenstein transform: $r(Y) = Y^3 - 7Y^2 + 14Y - 7$ satisfies $r(2X+2) = p(X)$, and $r$ is Eisenstein at $p=7$.

title: Algebraic Root Identities: The Galois Orbit of cos(π/7)
content:
The two root-image theorems are the algebraic heart of the proof, establishing that the three roots of p form a single cyclic Galois orbit.

**`root_image_gamma`** (CommRing): If p(α) = 0, then p(1−2α²) = 0. Proof: p(1−2a²) = (−8a³−4a²+4a+1)·p(a), which is zero when p(a)=0. Works in any CommRing — no characteristic hypothesis needed (no fractions appear).

**`root_image_beta`** (CharZero Field): If p(α) = 0, then p(2α²−α−1/2) = 0. Proof: p(2a²−a−1/2) = (8a³−8a²−2a+1)·p(a). The appearance of 1/2 requires CharZero: in characteristic 2 the expression is ill-defined.

Together, these generate the full orbit {cos(π/7), cos(3π/7), cos(5π/7)} from any single root, showing the Galois group acts transitively — which forces |Gal| = 3 (cyclic group ℤ/3ℤ).
mathContext:
Factor identities (proved by `ring` and `field_simp; ring`):
$$p(1-2\alpha^2) = (-8\alpha^3-4\alpha^2+4\alpha+1) \cdot p(\alpha)$$
$$p(2\alpha^2-\alpha-\tfrac{1}{2}) = (8\alpha^3-8\alpha^2-2\alpha+1) \cdot p(\alpha)$$

Root map cycle: $\cos(\pi/7) \xrightarrow{\gamma} \cos(5\pi/7) \xrightarrow{\gamma} \cos(3\pi/7) \xrightarrow{\gamma} \cos(\pi/7)$

title: Irreducibility via Eisenstein at 7 and Linear Substitution Transfer
content:
The irreducibility proof has three stages:

**Stage 1** (lines 85-118, ℤ): r = X³−7X²+14X−7 satisfies Eisenstein at p=7: (i) leading coeff 1 ∉ (7), (ii) coefficients −7, 14, −7 ∈ (7), (iii) constant −7 ∉ (49). Applied via `Polynomial.irreducible_of_eisenstein_criterion`.

**Stage 2** (lines 120-133, ℚ): Transfer via Gauss's lemma: `IsPrimitive.Int.irreducible_iff_irreducible_map_cast` converts ℤ-irreducibility to ℚ-irreducibility.

**Stage 3** (lines 134-200): The substitution ℓ = 2X+2 satisfies r(ℓ) = pCos7 (verified by `Polynomial.funext` + `ring`). Irreducibility transfers: if pCos7 = a·b, compose with the inverse ℓ⁻¹ = X/2−1 to factor r = (a∘ℓ⁻¹)·(b∘ℓ⁻¹), contradicting r's irreducibility. The compositional inverse ℓ·ℓ⁻¹ = X is verified explicitly by `interval_cases` on coefficients.
mathContext:
Eisenstein at $p=7$: $r = Y^3 - 7Y^2 + 14Y - 7$. The substitution $\ell = 2X+2$ with inverse $\ell^{-1} = X/2-1$ gives $r = r \circ X = r \circ (\ell \circ \ell^{-1}) = p_{\cos(7)} \circ \ell^{-1}$.

For cos(20°): $r' = Y^3 - 6Y^2 + 9Y - 3$ (Eisenstein at 3), same substitution $2X+2$.

title: Splitting Field = ℚ(α): The Factored Form Identity
content:
The key step is showing [SplittingField:ℚ] = 3. Strategy: prove all roots lie in ℚ(α).

**`root_in_sf`** = `rootOfSplits(...)` is a canonical root α in the splitting field. `root_is_root` and `root_eq_zero` establish p(α) = 0 and 8α³−4α��−4α+1 = 0.

**`factored_eval_eq`** (CharZero Field): The identity `p(a) − 8(a−α)(a−β)(a−γ) = (4αa−4α²+1)·p(α)` shows p factors completely as `8(a−α)(a−β)(a−γ)` when p(α)=0. This is the polynomial splitting identity.

**`rootSet_subset_adjoin`**: Every root of p in the splitting field equals α, β, or γ (case-split from factored form). Since β, γ ∈ ℚ(α) (verified by `IntermediateField.mul_mem`, `div_mem`, etc.), all roots are in ℚ(α).

**`adjoin_root_eq_top`** → **`splitting_finrank`**: Since all roots lie in ℚ(α), the splitting field equals ℚ(α). Then [SF:ℚ] = [ℚ(α):ℚ] = deg(minpoly α) = 3.
mathContext:
Key identity: $p(a) = 8(a-\alpha)(a-\beta)(a-\gamma)$ when $p(\alpha)=0$, with remainder $(4\alpha a - 4\alpha^2+1) \cdot p(\alpha)$.

Result: $\text{SplittingField}(p) = \mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$, so $[\text{SF}:\mathbb{Q}] = [\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] = \deg(\text{minpoly}(\alpha)) = 3$.

title: Main Theorem: |Gal| = 3 via card_of_separable
content:
The proof closes in three lines: `Polynomial.Gal.card_of_separable` states that for separable p, |Gal(p/ℚ)| = [SplittingField(p):ℚ]. `pCos7_separable` follows from `pCos7_irreducible` (irreducible polynomials over char 0 fields are automatically separable). `splitting_finrank` gives [SF:ℚ] = 3. Hence |Gal| = 3.

**Pattern**: For odd prime q, the minimal polynomial of cos(π/q) over ℚ has degree (q−1)/2, and its Galois group is cyclic of order (q−1)/2. The cos(π/7) case gives (7−1)/2 = 3; the cos(π/9) = cos(20°) case gives (9−1)/2 = 4... wait, no: for q=9 (not prime), the degree is φ(18)/2 = 3. For q=7: φ(14)/2 = 3. For q=11: φ(22)/2 = 5. This generalizes to |Gal(ℚ(cos(π/n))/ℚ)| = φ(2n)/2.

The divisibility section (lines 249-269, not used in the final proof) provides an independent check: 3 | |Gal| (via prime_degree_dvd_card) and |Gal| | 6 (via S₃ embedding), consistent with |Gal| = 3.
mathContext:
$$|\text{Gal}(p_{\cos(\pi/7)}/\mathbb{Q})| = [\text{SplittingField}(p_{\cos(\pi/7)}):\mathbb{Q}] = 3$$

General pattern for $n \geq 3$: $[\mathbb{Q}(\cos(\pi/n)):\mathbb{Q}] = \varphi(2n)/2$, where $\varphi$ is Euler's totient.
